author: lemire
body:
Follow-up to a review suggestion on the AVX2 popcount PR, applied to the NEON side.

## What

Each of the five NEON popcount routines opened its outer block loop by clamping the outstanding 64-byte-block count to `INNERMAX` with a compare and a forward branch:

```asm
	MOVD INNERMAX, R4
	CMP R4, R3
	BHS <label>
	MOVD R3, R4
<label>:
	SUB R4, R3, R3
```

This replaces that with a branch-free `CSEL` sequence, factored into a `SPLITBLOCKS` macro to sit alongside the file's existing `FOLD4`/`ZEROPART`/`DRAIN` macros:

```asm
	SUBS INNERMAX, R3, R6
	MOVD INNERMAX, R4
	CSEL CS, R4, R3, R4     // R4 = min(R3, INNERMAX)
	CSEL CS, R6, ZR, R3     // R3 = max(R3-INNERMAX, 0)
```

The `SUBS` computes the leftover count *and* sets the flags that choose between the two cases, so it is four instructions instead of five, branch-free, and it removes five now-unused labels (`slinner`, `andinner`, `orinner`, `xorinner`, `maskinner`).

`R6` is the scratch register rather than `R5`, because `R5` holds the slice length across the vector loop in the four two-input routines.

## Performance: none, and that is expected

This is a code-size/clarity change. The sequence runs once per `INNERMAX` batch; since a roaring bitmap container is 1024 words = 128 blocks and `INNERMAX` is 1024 blocks, that is **once per call**, against an inner loop that saturates the NEON pipes for ~280 cycles. Measured on an arm64 laptop, `-count 6`:

| benchmark | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `PopcntSlice1024NEON` | 70.3 ns/op | 69.8 ns/op |
| `PopcntAndSlice1024NEON` | 104.0 ns/op | 103.9 ns/op |

Both differences are inside run-to-run noise. Please do not merge this expecting a speedup.

## Testing

`go test ./...` passes on arm64, as does `go vet`.

⚠️ **Worth flagging: the existing tests do not cover this code path.** `neonTestLengths` tops out at 1025 words = 128 blocks, so the outer block loop never iterates more than once and the `CS` side of both `CSEL`s is never taken. I confirmed this by mutation: flipping `CSEL CS` to `CSEL CC` still passes `TestNEONPopcntDifferential`.

I verified this change locally with a temporary test at lengths that cross the batch boundary (8188/8191/8192/8193/8200, 16383–16385, 24576, 32775) plus an all-ones saturated case, differentially against the `popcnt*SliceGo` reference implementations. That temp test passes on this branch and fails on the mutant. It is **not** included here, since the request was to keep this PR to the `CSEL` change alone — happy to add it as a follow-up if you would like the coverage upstream.

author: nicolas-codemate
body:
## Summary

`pixelcast.yaml` est relu quand sa date de modification bouge, au lieu d'être mémorisé pour la vie du process : une édition prend effet au cycle de synchronisation suivant, sans redémarrer le conteneur. Son chemin devient configurable par `PIXELCAST_CONFIG_FILE`, ce qui permet au déploiement de monter un répertoire plutôt que le fichier — un montage mono-fichier reste accroché à l'inode et ne suivrait pas le `rename()` d'un éditeur, rendant la relecture inutile.

Une relecture qui échoue conserve la dernière configuration valide et le signale une fois dans les logs ; le tout premier chargement, lui, continue de lever et d'arrêter le consumer.

## Points d'attention

- **Rupture de déploiement.** Un hôte existant doit copier le nouveau `deploy/compose.yaml`, ajouter la ligne `PIXELCAST_CONFIG_FILE` à son `pixelcast.env`, puis `mkdir pixelcast-config && mv pixelcast.yaml pixelcast-config/`. La procédure est dans le README. `PIXELCAST_CONFIG_FILE` est la seule variable non commentée de `pixelcast.env.dist`, parce que le défaut `/app/pixelcast.yaml` tombe hors du nouveau montage : déplacer ce défaut dans `pixelcast-config/` supprimerait ce piège, au prix d'un `mv` dans chaque checkout de dev, et contredirait le ticket qui demande que le défaut reste inchangé. À arbitrer.
- **Portée de la relecture.** Les options d'un groupe (couleurs, items suivis, seuils) sont prises au cycle suivant. L'`interval`, le flag `enabled` et la fenêtre de veille passent par `Schedule::getSchedule()`, que le scheduler Symfony retient pour la vie du consumer : ils attendent son recyclage horaire. Documenté dans le README.

Closes #109

author: phroun
body:
Shrinking the SDL/WebGPU desktop loses windows off the edge. They do not come back when it grows.

## What broke

There are two paths that position a window, and only one knew about the provisional corral:

| path | geometry | corral |
|---|---|---|
| `WindowManager.Paint` — software renderer, TUI | `m.displayBounds(win)` | ✅ |
| `renderer_webgpu.go` — SDL/WebGPU compositor | `win.Bounds()` | ❌ |

The corral was written against the software paint loop, which was the only path at the time. The WebGPU renderer composites each window as a **layer of its own** and reads geometry through a locally-declared interface:

```go
type WindowLike interface {
	Bounds() core.UnitRect     // logical bounds — the corral is never consulted
	Paint(*core.Painter)
}
```

`grep displayBounds sdl/` returns nothing. The compositor has never heard of it.

Nothing was deleted, which is why it went unnoticed: every corral test drives `WindowManager` or `MDIPane` directly, and no test asks where a window landed on the compositor. `SoftwareRenderer.RenderFrameWithChildWindows` returns `"child window compositing not supported"` and falls back to the paint loop, so the TUI and the software renderer never showed it — only the WebGPU path does.

**The tell that confirms the diagnosis:** hit-testing *did* go through the container (`manager.go:2587` and friends all use `displayBounds`). So a window that had fallen off the edge was **clickable at the corralled position and inert where it appeared**. Draw and hit disagreed.

## The fix

The corral had to become readable from **outside** the container that computes it.

`Window.DisplayBounds()` asks a delegate the container installs; `WindowManager` and `MDIPane` both set it to their own `displayBounds`. One corral, not two implementations of one — the test asserts the window's answer and the container's are **equal**, rather than each separately plausible, because the disagreement *is* the failure.

The compositor asks through `displayBoundsOf`, an optional type assertion, so nothing that doesn't implement it stops matching — overlays and tear-off halos keep working unchanged.

Two cases answer with plain bounds, deliberately:
- **No container** — a torn-off window owns its OS geometry and has no corral to report. Returning an empty rect would erase it from the compositor.
- **Maximized** — it already tracks the client area; corralling would fight the container that just sized it.

## Tests

`test_manager_displaybounds_test.go` asks the corral question the way an outsider has to ask it — the hole the existing tests leave. Verified load-bearing: removing the delegate install fails it with exactly the reported bug,

```
shrunk: DisplayBounds {X:600 ...}, container draws {X:284 ...}
```

plus the two fallbacks above.

## Verification

```
GOWORK=off go build ./...                        # clean
GOWORK=off go vet ./...                          # clean
GOWORK=off go test ./...                         # all pass
GOWORK=off go {build,vet,test} -tags sdl ./...   # all clean
```

Default `-mod=readonly` throughout. `const Build` → **20**. No `go.mod`/`go.sum` change and no new dependency this time.

author: fastrevmd-lab
body:
Closes the question #21 was opened around. Documentation only.

## What the portal actually does

Captured live from the Devices page (non-destructively — the mutating calls were recorded and aborted before leaving the browser, so neither button fired):

| Purpose | Method and path | Body |
|---|---|---|
| SDC-side intended changes | `POST /configmgmt/view-ui-changes` | `{"device_uuid":"…"}` |
| Device-side out-of-band delta | `POST /configmgmt/view-device-changes` | `{"device_uuid":"…"}` |
| Both buttons | `POST /configmgmt/resolve-oob` | `{"device_uuid":"…","accept_device_change":<bool>}` |

**`accept_device_change: false` deletes the out-of-band change from the device.** "Reject" edits the device rather than discarding SDC's opinion. That distinction is recorded prominently, because anything exposing this later must make the two impossible to confuse.

## Why the search kept failing

These are `/configmgmt/*` on the **portal host**, not `/api/v1/*` on the API host. They were never in the vendored spec's surface, so no amount of searching it would have found them. Worth remembering as a property of this API's documentation: the spec covers the public REST surface only, and the product has more than that.

## Why this server cannot use them

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `POST /configmgmt/view-device-changes` with `x-api-key` | `403` |
| the same with **no auth at all** | `403` — identical |
| `POST /api/v1/configmgmt/view-device-changes` with `x-api-key` | `404` |

The key and no key give the same answer, so the credential buys nothing there. The `404` is the useful contrast: `/api/v1` is routed and has no such path, while `/configmgmt/*` is a surface this credential cannot reach at all.

Implementing it would mean holding a user's web session and calling undocumented BFF endpoints that can change without notice. That is the wrong trade for a management plane, so the conclusion is that clearing drift is **a portal action with no API equivalent** — a property of the product, not a gap here.

`docs/operations.md` now says so where an operator meets the problem, including that `prepare_sdc_policy_deploy` and device sync are both *not* substitutes.

## Evidence trail

`docs/sdc-api/README.md` §12 carries the full capture and the auth probe, so the next person does not repeat the search. If Juniper later exposes an equivalent under `/api/v1` or `/api/v2`, the captured semantics are the ground truth for what the buttons do.

body:
## Wat doet deze wijziging?
**De poort bestond, maar hij was vrijwillig.** `scripts/lint/lint-web.ps1` draait `tsc --noEmit` plus
`npm run build` en is sinds 2026-07-26 de laatste wacht vóór een live deploy — maar hij draaide alleen
lokaal, en alleen als iemand `open-pr` gebruikte. Een PR uit de GitHub-UI, een vergeten `-SkipLint`, een
merge op een moment van haast: er stond niets tussen. In een repo waar een merge rechtstreeks naar
`djcylow.com` deployt en er geen staging is, was dat het grootste gat in de keten. Dit was ook het eerste
openstaande punt dat `docs/gelijktrekken-met-de-bron` bij zijn afsluiting neerlegde.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` sluit dat gat: op **elke** PR en elke push naar `main` draait dezelfde poort
server-side.

#### Hetzelfde script, geen tweede kopie

De workflow schrijft tsc en de build niet over maar roept `lint-web.ps1` aan. Dat is een geleende les uit
de bron, die er expliciet over is: zijn CI hield tot 7 augustus 2026 een inline kopie van de testloop, en
die bleef dagenlang serieel draaien nadat beide lokale aanroepers al geparallelliseerd waren — *"the copy
nobody looks at being the one that drifts."* Eén poort betekent hier dat de ESLint-stap die in het script
als TODO staat, straks op beide plekken tegelijk aangaat.

#### Ubuntu, waar de bron windows kiest — en dat is het inhoudelijke punt

De bron draait zijn CI op `windows-latest`, met reden: zijn scripts targeten Windows PowerShell 5.1 en het
geteste product zíjn die scripts. Hier is het geteste product de site, en **Netlify bouwt op Linux**. Dat
verschil is niet cosmetisch:

> Een import met de verkeerde letterkast — `./header` terwijl het bestand `Header.tsx` heet — bouwt
> probleemloos op het case-insensitieve bestandssysteem van Windows en **breekt op Netlify**. Precies de
> klasse fout die de lokale poort structureel niet kan zien, en die meteen de live site raakt omdat er
> geen staging tussen zit.

Daarom draait de poort op `ubuntu-latest` met `shell: pwsh`. Dat maakt de CI-run strikt strenger dan de
lokale, wat de goede richting is voor een laatste wacht.

**Dat vroeg één aanpassing in het script**, want het was met PowerShell 5.1-aannames geschreven: PowerShell
7 kan een native commando met een exitcode ≠ 0 als terminating error gooien zodra
`PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference` aanstaat, en dit script beoordeelt `tsc` en de build juist bewust
op `$LASTEXITCODE` om zijn eigen samenvatting te kunnen printen. Zonder die ingreep blokkeerde de poort nog
steeds, maar met een ruwe exception in plaats van *"de build faalt — mergen zou een kapotte site
opleveren"*. De guard is versie-veilig (PS 5.1 kent de variabele niet), en het script is lokaal onder 5.1
opnieuw groen gedraaid.

#### Wat dit wél en niet oplost — en waarom de PR-regel niet meebeweegt

De PR-regel van vanochtend verantwoordde zijn ruime uitzondering met de meting *"de bron-default leunt op de
lint gate, the test gate, and CI; hier bestaan twee van die drie niet"*, en beloofde: **komt er ooit CI, dan
is dat het moment om de grens opnieuw te wegen.** Die CI is er nu — en de grens is toch niet verschoven. Dat
is een besluit, geen vergeten stap:

- Er zijn nog steeds **nul testsuites**. De poort bewijst dat het **bouwt**, niet dat het gedrag gelijk
  bleef, en al helemaal niet dat een pagina er goed uitziet.
- Er is **geen branch protection**. Zonder die instelling is de run een **signaal, geen slot**: `gh pr merge`
  mergt een PR met een rode CI zonder morren. Dat aanzetten is een repo-setting en dus Dave's woord.

Van de drie pijlers staan er nu dus twee. Het herwegen van de grens tussen "wacht op Dave" en "loopt door"
is daarmee een openstaande beslissing van Dave geworden in plaats van een hypothetische — en dat staat nu
zo in `CLAUDE.md`, in Chris' lens en in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, op de plekken waar tot vandaag *"er is geen CI"*
als vaststaand feit werd aangevoerd. Ook de `Get-PrMergeMethod`-verantwoording in `repo-config.ps1` is
bijgewerkt: die noemde twee redenen om `ship-pr` te mijden en voorspelde zelf dat reden 1 zou vervallen
zodra er CI kwam. Dat is nu gebeurd; reden 2 blijft.

#### Eén ding dat de workflow bewust níet vastlegt

Deze repo pint zijn Node-versie **nergens** vast: geen `.nvmrc`, geen `.node-version`, geen `engines`, geen
`NODE_VERSION` in `netlify.toml`. Netlify draait dus zijn eigen default en CI de versie in de workflow (22,
gelijk aan wat hier lokaal draait). Die twee kunnen uit elkaar lopen zonder dat iets dat meldt, en dan
bewijst de CI-build iets anders dan wat live gaat. De reparatie is een `.nvmrc` — maar Netlify **leest** dat
bestand, dus het toevoegen ervan verandert de live build. Dat is een beslissing van Dave en staat als
comment in de workflow genoteerd, niet stilletjes uitgevoerd.

#### Meegenomen: de i18n-verwijzing die vandaag dood raakte

`feature/i18n-setup` is op 2026-08-13 gesloten (Dave: liep 272 commits achter, er gebeurt niets meer mee),
gearchiveerd als tag `archive/feature-i18n-setup` op `origin` — dezelfde conventie als
`archive/feature-cookie-banner`. `CLAUDE.md` verwees op twee plekken naar die branch als "geparkeerd", en
dat is nu onjuist; beide wijzen naar de tag, met de kanttekening dat opnieuw beginnen goedkoper is dan
rebasen over 272 commits Next-upgrades. Dat hoort strikt genomen in een eigen branch, maar het raakt
dezelfde regels van `CLAUDE.md` als het werk hierboven en zou daar als merge-conflict terugkomen.

## Type wijziging
- [ ] Nieuwe feature/pagina (`feature/`)
- [ ] Bugfix (`fix/`)
- [ ] Mix data (`data/`)
- [ ] Content/tekst (`content/`)
- [ ] Styling/CSS (`style/`)
- [ ] Docs (`docs/`)
- [x] Config/tooling (`config/`)

## Checklist

author: mintedxmorphy
body: ## Why Fine Mess snaps back Dragging **Fine Mess** to the top of Queue was failing for two stacked reasons in the production board. **1. The top of Queue is covered by the stretched-job overlay.** Stretched jobs render in a full-width overlay (`z-index: 20`) that sits on top of every column, including Queue. That overlay is drop-disabled. Dropping a card on the “#1” spot therefore often arrived as: - no destination at all → `onDragEnd` returned immediately and the card animated back to spot 5 - or a drop on the overlay, which the old fallback treated as “append at the end of the column” If Queue only has 5 jobs (or Fine Mess is already last), appending to the end leaves it in the 5th spot. Same visual: it snaps back. **2. “Move to top” order math could not beat the current #1 job.** Even when the drop registered, the new `dashboard_order` was `Math.max(0.5, firstJobOrder - 1)`. Once the top job already had order `0.5`, the next “move to top” also got `0.5`. The board then ties on order and sorts by customer/matrix name, so Fine Mess jumped back to wherever that name sorts (e.g. 5th). ## What changed - Column droppables now include the station header, so dropping on “Queue” counts as index 0. - Overlay / empty-destination drops reuse the last real column hover (or index 0), instead of cancelling or appending at the bottom. - Top-of-column inserts always get an order strictly above the current first card (`next / 2`). If that still would not sort into the intended slot, the column is reindexed `1..n`. - Airtable stage/order writes use `typecast: true` so fractional orders persist. After deploy, drag Fine Mess onto the Queue header or above the current #1 card — it should stay at the top.

Previously, the script referenced `./node_modules/.bin/electron-rebuild.cmd`, which only exists on Windows environments. This broke execution on Linux/macOS, where yarn generate binary symlinks without the `.cmd` extension.

## What is the current behavior?

Clicking "generate" on the configuration page without any selected expansion
navigates away instead of reporting the problem. The button is a plain
`routerLink="/set"`, so the navigation is always started and only cancelled
afterwards by the `configurationGuard`. That guard calls `router.navigate()`
while also returning `false`, which starts a second navigation while the first
one is still being cancelled and leaves the user on an unpredictable page.

## What is the new behavior?

Generating without a selected expansion keeps the user on the configuration
page and reports a validation error.

-   The generate button now runs `ConfigurationComponent.generate()`, which
    validates the edition form group before navigating to `/set`.
-   `EditionSelectComponent` shows the error itself: it paints its checkboxes
    and labels in the warn color, renders "Choose at least one expansion" below
    the "all" checkbox and scrolls itself into view, so the error is visible
    even when the user has scrolled down to the button. The error state is
    driven by the existing `validateMinSelect` validator and clears as soon as
    an expansion is selected.
-   `configurationGuard` returns a `UrlTree` instead of `router.navigate()` plus
    `false`, so the redirect for direct visits to `/set` is deterministic.

The `errorMessage` of the expansions step could not be used for this case: the
CDK only renders a step's error state while the step is **not** selected, and
without a selected expansion no special card type is available, so the special
cards step is not rendered at all and the expansions step is always the
selected one.

author: algb20
body:
Vercel's Hobby plan allows two cron jobs, each at most once per day. An expression that fires more often is not throttled and does not warn — the whole deployment fails:

```
Hobby accounts are limited to daily cron jobs. This cron expression
(0 */6 * * *) would run more than once per day.
```

I committed a six-hourly publish schedule, and from that moment **every Vercel build for this project failed**. Nothing about the application was broken; the site simply stopped receiving new code. The symptom was "I merged and nothing changed" — a hosting failure wearing an application failure's costume — and it cost most of a day to find, because the site kept serving perfectly well, just the old build.

## The fix

Two crons, both daily. The Radar's two halves are combined into `/api/cron/radar` rather than scheduled separately, because two halves would spend both of the plan's slots and leave none for publishing.

## So it cannot repeat

`vercel-config.test.ts` asserts:

- no more crons than the plan allows
- every schedule fires at most once a day
- every cron points at a job the route actually implements
- no two crons contend for the same minute

The predicate is tested against the exact expression that broke it.

## The cadence isn't lost, it moved

`netlify/functions/scheduled-jobs.mts` still runs every six hours, and Netlify is where this project deploys. Both schedulers call the same `/api/cron/<job>` routes, so the work is identical and only the cadence differs — a plan limit, not a product decision.

`vercel.json.md` records the reasoning next to the file, since the file itself is six lines that look arbitrary without it.

## Verification

696 tests pass; typecheck clean.

body:
20 commits, each its own logical change with its own `code_version`. Rebased onto main at v1.0.732 (the branch had drifted 61 commits behind production — see the merge note at the end).

> **Bundling note.** `CLAUDE.md` PROMOTION RULES item 5 wants one logical change per PR. The session is pinned to one designated branch, so several land together. They stay separable the way attribution actually needs: **distinct commits, distinct version bumps, distinct rollback triggers.** Flagging rather than quietly bundling.

---

## 1. The camera could not cross a pole — fixed (v1.0.692)

**Human report:** *"when looking at the moon it will not let you go over the axis of rotation like over the poles same thing on the earth ... I came across this issue when looking at the bottom of the moon to see the missions."*

**Root cause, one line of vector math.** `camBasis` derived the camera's up-vector from a *constant world axis* every frame, so `cross(f, upRef) → 0` as the view approached that axis — the basis degenerates at the pole and snaps to an arbitrary fallback. Rather than remove the singularity, the code fenced it off with a clamp, and **the fence is what the user hit**:

| state | allowed polar range |
|---|---|
| lock ON (**the default**) | 6.88° … **114.06°** |
| lock OFF | 2.86° … 177.14° |

On the default the camera stopped **66° short of the Moon's south pole** — and Chang'e 4/6, LCROSS, IM-1 and Chandrayaan-3 all sit inside that unreachable cap.

**Fix:** stop *deriving* the up-vector, start **carrying** it — parallel-transport along the view's own rotation, re-orthonormalise. Continuous everywhere including at the pole, so the singularity is gone rather than fenced. `setDir()` is now the only place `dir` changes, so orbit drags *and* discrete re-anchors (flight arrival, focus release) all carry the up through the change.

**The polar clamp is deleted**, along with `polarClampDots` and its four constants.

`lockHorizon` is **re-scoped, not removed**: it no longer bounds where the camera may go, only whether the horizon re-levels — and it releases only inside a small cap where "level" is genuinely undefined. This preserves the human's 2026-07-19 *"level, not tilted/wonky"* directive for normal viewing while satisfying the new one.

**A test that pinned the bug was removed, deliberately and on the record.** `"polarClampDots: lock forbids under-ecliptic, unlock only widens"` asserted `"poles excluded even unlocked"` — the defect itself. Replaced by five stronger tests, notably a **400-step sweep that walks the camera over the pole asserting the up-vector never jumps >0.05**, and orthonormality asserted **at `(0,0,±1)` exactly** — the input that used to hit the degenerate fallback.

---

## 2. "All power grids" silently skipped Asia (v1.0.693)

**Human:** *"What about China or russia we dont seem to have anything on them"* … *"when i turn on all power grids i dont see it them"* — with a screenshot showing the master switch **on**, Europe lit, China/India/Russia dark.

`GRID_MASTER_IDS` listed four continents. Asia had shipped **end to end** — registry live, client wired, `power_asia.pmtiles` serving HTTP 206 — but its id was never appended. The panel subtitle printed the bug on screen: *"US · Canada · S. America · Europe."*

**What was hidden** (measured from live PMTiles metadata):

| | features | file |
|---|---:|---:|
| United States | 9,193,886 | 26.3 MB |
| **China** | **4,276,317** | 89.6 MB |
| **Russia** | **3,131,036** | 76.2 MB |
| Germany | 1,327,939 | 38.9 MB |

China and Russia are the **two largest single-country files in the bucket**, each bigger than the entire US set, and both unreachable from the control that claims to show *"every grid mapped so far."*

> I first diagnosed this as discoverability (236 layers, no search box). **That was wrong**, and the user's screenshot falsified it — the switch was already on. Recorded in `experiments.md` rather than quietly replaced.

**Ratchet:** two tests make the *registry* the source of truth — every layer named `/Power Grid \(all/` with `status: "live"` must be in `GRID_MASTER_IDS`. Verified by deleting the Asia line (5 pass / 1 fail with the exact diagnostic) and restoring.

---

## 3. Africa + Oceania: 78 layers built, served, and unreachable (v1.0.695)

The Asia repair surfaced this: `power_africa`, `power_oceania` and 76 per-country tiles were **built, uploaded and serving HTTP 206 from production** with no registry entry and no client wiring. We were paying to store and serve two continents nobody could reach.

The work-list came from the **bucket**, not from guessing — pure wiring, zero pipeline runs, zero new data.

**Two ambiguities resolved by measurement** (reading PMTiles headers over the wire, not inferring from filenames):
- `power_af_sn` and `power_af_sngm` have **identical bboxes** (Senegal + Gambia) but differ in depth — **z0..11 vs z0..9**. `sngm` is a stale lower-fidelity duplicate: wired `sn`, excluded `sngm`, left a comment so nobody "fixes" the apparent omission.
- `af_ic` = Canary Islands, `af_sh` = St Helena/Ascension/Tristan da Cunha, `oc_us` = Guam/American Samoa/N. Marianas.

**The ratchet worked.** The parity test added hours earlier caught both new continents *automatically*, the moment their registry entries landed and before any wiring existed:

```
live continental master(s) missing from GRID_MASTER_IDS:
powergrid_africa, powergrid_oceania          # pass 5 / fail 1
```

That is the Asia bug class being **prevented** rather than re-diagnosed.

**Verified:** probed all 78 referenced tiles against the live production proxy — every one returns real PMTiles magic bytes, zero broken layers. Also added a **bucket ↔ registry parity test**, the stronger invariant this bug class kept demanding.

**Honesty rail:** every new description states that OSM coverage varies and that **sparse rendering means thinly mapped, not absent on the ground**. Africa's density is genuinely uneven and the continental master says so outright.

---

## 4. Moon: our own tile pyramid, and the fuzz fix (v1.0.689 / v1.0.690 / v1.0.691)

**3a — Law II.8** (*"runtime never touches an upstream WMTS"*). `scripts/moon_bake.py` bakes LROC WAC from the **original USGS public-domain source** (5.55 GiB) into R2, in the exact Trek EQ scheme `lroc.ts` already implements. **Full native set shipped: 43,690 tiles, z0–z7, $0, no RunPod** (ledger untouched at $43.12). Verified visually — 8 independently-baked tiles restitched into a seamless globe, correct orientation, polar illumination gaps preserved as real nodata.

Trek's own z8 is an **upsample** of this same 100 m/px product, so our native ceiling is z7; the manifest flags anything above it and a test pins it.

**Cross-language contract:** the bake writes keys in Python, the client computes URLs in TypeScript — a mismatch fails *silently at runtime* (404s / black Moon). `test_moon_bake.py` **parses `lroc.ts`** and asserts the formulas and `{z}/{y}/{x}` row-before-column order still agree.

**3b — the fuzz.** `MOON_PATCH_COVER_MARGIN = 2.8` inflated the requested span 7.8× in area (only ~36% ever on screen), and the planner dropped whole **zoom levels** to fit the 2048px cap. body:
# fix(charset): use true Windows-1252 encoding for WIN1252

## Summary

This fixes Firebird `WIN1252` connections by routing them through the existing
ICU/WHATWG `windows-1252` codec instead of Node.js `latin1`.

It also:

- Keeps `ISO8859_1` and `LATIN1` on their existing Latin-1 mapping.
- Covers SQL text, parameters, returned text columns, and textual BLOBs through
  the existing codec path.
- Preserves byte-for-byte `Buffer` pass-through.
- Throws a descriptive error when a requested ICU codepage is unavailable,
  instead of silently falling back to UTF-8.
- Updates the charset documentation and examples.
- Adds unit and Firebird integration regression tests.

## Why this is needed

Windows-1252 and ISO-8859-1/Node.js `latin1` are not equivalent.

They differ particularly in the `0x80`-`0x9F` range. Windows-1252 uses this
range for characters including:

- `€`
- Smart quotes
- En and em dashes
- `Œ/œ`
- `Š/š`
- `Ž/ž`
- `™`
- `Ÿ`

With the current `WIN1252` to `latin1` mapping, these characters are encoded
to incorrect bytes when written and are returned as control characters when
real Windows-1252 bytes are read.

For example, this string does not round-trip correctly with the current
mapping:

```text
€ “Windows” — Œuvre ™ ŠŽŸ
```

This affects databases genuinely declared as `WIN1252`. 

## Implementation

- Adds `WIN1252: 'windows-1252'` to the existing ICU codec table.
- Removes `WIN1252` from the native Node.js `latin1` mapping.
- Leaves `ISO8859_1`, `LATIN1`, and `NONE` unchanged.
- Uses the existing codepage codec implementation and cache.
- Fails explicitly if a constrained Node.js runtime lacks a requested ICU
  codec, rather than encoding the text as UTF-8.

## Tests

Coverage includes:

- Exact encoding and decoding of the defined printable Windows-1252
  characters in the `0x80`-`0x9F` range.
- Verification that Windows-1252 extension bytes are not interpreted as
  ISO-8859-1.
- Case-insensitive codec lookup and caching.

author: us
body:
Two independent fixes found by auditing four days of production logs
(2026-08-09 → 08-12, 20,012 successful scrapes and 13,443 engine traces).

## 1. Registrar parking pages were billed as content

A parking page is HTTP 200 carrying a few hundred to a few thousand bytes of
clean markdown, so it cleared both shared gates: `ScrapeData::http_error()`
returns early on the status, and `classify_block`'s markdown-substantial guard
returns `None` before `antibot::classify` runs at all. **294 of 20,012
production successes** were parking, marketplace or holding pages delivered and
billed as content.

The verdict is anchored on **the page naming its own host**. Unanchored template
literals were tried and rejected: every nginx install tutorial quotes the default
vhost verbatim, "Apache2 Ubuntu Default Page" is the title of a common
StackOverflow thread, and UDRP decisions say "this domain has been registered".
A bare token match is no better — "Insurance.com is for sale" is a real headline,
and the pattern also accepts `checkout.html` or `main.py`. Requiring the token to
equal the scraped host rejects all of them, and on the corpus the anchor cost
nothing: the token equalled the host in all 294, and it correctly rejected two
pages that named a different domain.

`under construction` and `coming soon` are **deliberately out of scope** — those
are states an origin published on purpose, so they stay truthful scrapes and stay
billable. That is 68% of the flagged population, so this does not take the class
to zero by design.

Reported as `no_usable_content`, not `anti_bot`: telling a customer that a domain
which is for sale was blocked by anti-bot is what sends them to buy proxies for a
site that does not exist.

## 2. A blackholed origin was reported as our timeout

When the direct egress hit a connect-phase timeout the fallback proxy was armed,
and a connect-level failure on that proxy exited as `HttpError` because the
verdict required `!use_proxy`. The JS ladder only short-circuits on
`TargetUnreachable`, so a host with no listening socket was handed every tier's
full budget: **~38s per request across ~1,050 requests/day**, returned as a 504
telling the caller to raise a timeout that cannot help, and paging the 5xx
watchdog as our outage rather than their dead target. Requests that do land in
`target_unreachable` today finish at **p50 2,573ms** — the same verdict arriving
on time.

`direct_connect_failed` is narrowed at its source so both arms that read it
inherit one meaning, and it now requires that the origin never answered at all.
A refused or reset proxy still stays 502, because a refusal is not a timeout.

## Benchmark impact — measured, not assumed

The parking verdict is the only change here that can move scrape-success, so it
was gated against the frozen 1,000-URL set before merge rather than after. Only
rows that are currently `ok=true` **and** under the new 16 KB body ceiling
**and** found no expected content can flip — 277 of them. Those were re-scraped
through the live API and the shipped predicate applied offline, three times.

**Result: exactly one row flips, `https://ccg.ai`**, whose `<h1>` is literally
`# ccg.ai is for sale!` served at ccg.ai. Raw scrape-success 877 → 876. The
dead-link-adjusted figure is unchanged, since that URL is a dead link by any
definition.

Nothing here touches render timing, so p50/p90 and truth-recall are unaffected.

## Verification

- 1,619 workspace tests, clippy `-D warnings` clean, fmt clean
- The shipped Rust predicate was cross-checked against an independently written
  reference over all 20,012 corpus documents: 294 matches, zero disagreement
- Reviewed to consensus over two rounds by three independent reviewers; the first
  round's blockers (unanchored literals, a truncating capture, a too-tight
  budget) are all resolved here
- A third change — clamping the JS ladder for confirmed-dead origins — was
  **dropped from this PR**: production data shows 22% of chrome-failover
  successes take longer than the proposed budget, so it traded recall for
  latency. The right fix there is a host-level breaker, tracked separately.

author: ronaldrn
body:
## Description

This pull request adds a new `google-colab/` directory containing **four Jupyter notebooks** that provide a Google Colab workflow for preparing ERA5 data and running ATMOS-BUD.

The main workflow is:

```text
Access_to_Reanalysis_ERA5.ipynb
              ↓
       ERA5 NetCDF file
              ↓
      track_file.ipynb
              ↓
 track_<cyclone_name>.txt
              ↓
ATMOSBUD_Google_Colab.ipynb
              ↓
        ATMOS-BUD -t
              ↓
   Atmospheric budget results
```

The workflow is designed for cyclone-following applications using the ATMOS-BUD `-t` option. The ERA5 NetCDF file and the cyclone track file must contain matching dates and time steps.

### Added notebooks

* `Access_to_Reanalysis_ERA5.ipynb`
  Downloads and prepares the ERA5 meteorological fields required as input for ATMOS-BUD.

* `track_file.ipynb`
  Creates the `track_<cyclone_name>.txt` file containing the cyclone position and analysis-domain dimensions for each time step.

* `ATMOSBUD_Google_Colab.ipynb`
  Provides step-by-step instructions for installing and running ATMOS-BUD on Google Colab, including the use of the `-t` option for a moving domain that follows the cyclone.

* `Synoptic_chart_Reanalysis_ERA5.ipynb`
  Provides a complementary tool for generating synoptic charts from ERA5 reanalysis data, following the general visualization style of the synoptic maps developed by Alicia M. Bentley.

The synoptic-chart notebook is optional and is not required for the ATMOS-BUD calculations.

### Documentation

A `README.md` file was also added to the `google-colab/` directory describing the recommended workflow, input requirements, temporal consistency between ERA5 and track files, and the purpose of each notebook.

### Motivation

The goal of this contribution is to provide an additional cloud-based workflow for ATMOS-BUD, making the software easier to use in teaching, training, and research environments where a local installation may not be available.

The notebooks do not modify the core ATMOS-BUD source code.

author: danielhanchen
body:
## The symptom

Fine-tuning `unsloth/gemma-4-E2B-it` on a T4 with `use_gradient_checkpointing = "unsloth"` dies in the second step:

```
AssertionError: Something went unexpectedly wrong in activation checkpoint.
Please report this bug by filing an issue to PyTorch.
```

Shortly before it, unsloth_zoo prints its own warning naming `Gemma4RMSNorm.forward (scaled)` as having run out of recompilation cache. That warning is a red herring, and chasing it is what made this take a while.

## The mechanism

The recompile budget is the mechanism, but the budget that runs out belongs to no kernel we compile. Instrumenting torch's own `exceeds_recompile_limit` on the failing kernel:

```
EXHAUST reason=recompile_limit code=__setitem__ @/usr/lib/python3.12/weakref.py:427
        entries=1024 frame_id=11 frame_compile_id=1024 limit=1024 thread=Dummy-5

FINAL-TOP [('__setitem__ @weakref.py:427', 1030),
           ('_gemma4_rms_norm_scaled @gemma4_float32.py:296', 6),
           ('Gemma4ClippableLinear_forward', 4), ('apply_rotary_pos_emb', 4), ...]
```

`weakref.__setitem__` was compiled **1030 times in that one step** against a `recompile_limit` of 1024. The gemma4 RMSNorm kernel the warning names was compiled **six times in the whole run**.

Non-reentrant activation checkpointing recomputes each packed forward during backward and tracks the saved intermediates through weakly-keyed bookkeeping. That runs on the autograd thread with a compiled region on the stack, so Dynamo intercepts it, and it sees a fresh key object per checkpointed region: one compilation each, a thousand of them, not one of which can ever be reused. When the budget finally goes, the failure surfaces inside whichever compiled kernel was running, **after** that kernel has already run and its activations have been packed. `_retry_with_more_budget` then buys 16 more and re-invokes the same call, the retry packs the same activations a second time, and torch's recomputation hook trips `_internal_assert` on the duplicate.

That also explains the 62 to 72 second first step: most of it is spent compiling weak-dictionary inserts.

## The fix

Ask Dynamo not to compile them. `stop_compiling_weak_dictionary_writes()` marks four code objects skipped through `torch._dynamo.eval_frame.skip_code`, and `patch_torch_compile` calls it where Dynamo is already being configured and before anything compiles:

```
WeakKeyDictionary.__setitem__      WeakKeyDictionary.__delitem__
WeakValueDictionary.__setitem__    WeakValueDictionary.__delitem__
```

A skipped frame runs in the interpreter, which is what it did before anything thought to compile it, so this has no semantics of its own. Compiling a weak-dictionary insert buys nothing in the first place. Every failure to read torch's internals degrades to "nothing marked" rather than an error, since this runs at import.

The budget is then never touched, no retry happens, nothing is packed twice, and **the model stays compiled**. That is what separates this from the two workarounds that get the run to finish by turning compilation off.

## Two designs I tried first, and why they lose

Both assume the exhausted budget belongs to a kernel we compile. It does not.

**Raise the budget.** It is already 1024, raised from torch's default of 8 by `patching_utils`, and the demand was 1030 in a single step. The demand is one compilation per checkpointed region, so it scales with depth and sequence length. No fixed cap is enough, and a cap that were enough would still be paying for a thousand compilations nobody wants.

**Predict the exhaustion at a step boundary and go eager before it.** I built this and measured it on the T4. It never fired, and the run asserted exactly as before: the frame that overruns is created **during** the failing step and reaches 1024 compiles inside it, so nothing measured at the previous boundary can see it coming. The premise that 504 RMSNorm instances make the collision knowable in advance is also wrong, since those 504 instances share one code object that compiles six times.

## Evidence

One Kaggle T4 image throughout: `torch 2.10.0+cu128`, capability (7,5), `bf16 = false`, transformers 5.5.0, three steps of `unsloth/LaTeX_OCR`.

| kernel | zoo under test | result |
|---|---|---|
| `unsloth-t4-ci-7b86fbd2` | main | ASSERTED |
| `unsloth-t4-ci-a6eb18b9` | main | ASSERTED |
| `unsloth-t4-ci-934d681d` | main, instrumented | ASSERTED, named `weakref.__setitem__` x1030 |
| `unsloth-t4-ci-e29ca7f0` | main plus the skip only | COMPLETED, `[5.1565, 3.4462, 3.2893]` |
| `unsloth-t4-ci-8bbcc702` | this branch | COMPLETED, `[5.1565, 3.4462, 3.2885]`, 77.0 s |

Reference losses with `UNSLOTH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1`: `[5.1558, 3.4465, 3.3079]`. In the passing runs the per-frame compile counts are identical at every step boundary and `weakref.__setitem__` is absent entirely, so compilation is intact.

## Healthy path

`unsloth/gemma-3-270m-it`, LoRA, unsloth gradient checkpointing, 20 steps, ragged lengths, one B200. Three alternating pairs, warmup dropped, steady-state step time:

| | mean step (s) | median step (s) |
|---|---|---|
| main | 0.1662, 0.1709, 0.1690 | 0.1694, 0.1740, 0.1729 |
| this branch | 0.1660, 0.1659, 0.1669 | 0.1704, 0.1698, 0.1708 |

Mean of means 0.1687 against 0.1663. Losses identical to four decimals, and `eager_fallback_state()` reports nothing eager and nothing latched on either side, so no compilation was lost. The change costs nothing per step by construction: one mark on four code objects at import.

## Tests

`tests/test_weak_dictionary_writes_not_compiled.py`, 8 tests, CPU, milliseconds. All 8 fail on `main` and pass here. They pin which code objects are marked, that the writes still work, idempotence, that one refusal does not stop the others, that a torch without the accessor is not an import error, and that `patch_torch_compile` is wired to call it.

Full suite on this branch: 4969 passed, 212 skipped, exit 0.

## Known gap, worth a follow-up

The retry in `_retry_with_more_budget` is unsafe under a checkpoint in general: a recompile-limit failure can be raised for somebody else's frame after our own call has already packed activations, and re-invoking the call packs them twice. This removes the only trigger seen in the wild, but the same double-pack would happen for any other frame Dynamo intercepts from a saved-tensor hook.

## Not verified

Dynamo compiling `weakref.__setitem__` has only been observed on the T4, inside a checkpoint recompute on an autograd thread. Compiling that method directly on a local B200 produces no cache entries with or without the mark, so the tests pin the invariant after the mark rather than the failure itself. The offending line is `weakref.py:427` on python 3.12, which is `WeakKeyDictionary.__setitem__`; the other three are marked because they are the same class of thing and because that is the set the passing run was measured with.

## Tapping a sculpture now opens it

On a portfolio the photograph *is* the product, and a 340px tile is not a look at a sculpture. A piece now opens full size in a dark room with its number, its material, and **the phone number to call about that specific piece** — a visitor who's just decided they want one shouldn't have to scroll back up the page to find out how.

- **Contained, never cropped** — same rule as the grid.
- **Arrow keys and on-screen arrows** step along the row, wrapping at the ends, so someone can go through the work without returning to the grid each time.
- **Escape closes**, the backdrop closes, the plate itself doesn't.
- **Body scroll locks** while open and is restored after — otherwise the page drifts behind the overlay on a phone, and a leaked lock leaves the page stuck.
- On a phone the side arrows were squeezed into the gutter and half off-screen; there they drop below the plate as real tap targets.
- The caption follows the grid's rule: only what he actually told us. No title, no title line.

Three tests: the viewer opens with a `tel:` link naming the piece and carrying his number, it steps and wraps between pieces, and Escape closes it *and releases the scroll lock*.

The header cube, the **JP STUDIO** wordmark and the breadcrumb now take the colour of the tool you're in — green in Joint Printing, **blue in Webworks**, violet in Atom. Client Manager's own chrome (section icon, spinner, action links and their hovers) is Webworks blue.

body:
Closes `M130c` — item 17, the last of the pentest arc's Tier 2. `tests/api/identity/authz-generated.tflw` sits beside the **untouched** `authz.tflw` and asks tflw's authorization matcher for the same claims the hand-written control asserts by hand. Agreement is the invariant; keeping the control unported is what lets a future disagreement be a finding about the generator rather than a merge conflict.

It reverses two deliberate prior decisions, both knowingly:

- **D291/M128c** kept `authorized target` in the acceptance corpus only — refusal in the dogfood suite, permission in the corpus. Env `local` now declares one. The pairing survives: the `.checkonly` fixture still demonstrates the refusal (see `M130-08` below).
- **D318** kept `privileged` out of the root config for a *sequencing* reason — a config carrying unshipped grammar is red — and that reason was spent when `fe13960` landed on tflw `main`.

## `M130-06` — why three sessions need `privileged`, not one

With only `admin` marked, this file reported **two critical `sec/authz-object-leak` findings**, against `oauthLong` and `oauthShort`.

They are not real. `apiV2/src/oauth/oauth.service.ts:27` signs the client-credentials grant **for the seeded admin user** — "the admin service account" — so both tokens carry `role: ADMIN`, and `findOneScoped` admits them for exactly the reason it admits `admin`. Nothing in either session declaration says so; the fact lives in the server's grant code, which a suite author may not own.

**Every piece of evidence in those two findings was accurate** — a real id, really served, to a real non-owner, with a runnable repro. Only knowing what the grant mints separates that from a genuine BOLA, which is precisely the knowledge this tier exists to substitute for. That makes the false positive self-confirming rather than obviously wrong, and it is the shape worth carrying into the guide.

So: `privileged` is a claim about an identity's *authority*, and authority cannot be read off a session declaration. You find it by running the tier and asking, per principal, whether the access it demonstrated is a role fact or a bug. All three marked; **2/2 green**.

(`privileged` goes *after* `oauth2` — `TF010` says so and says why: the modifier is read last so `oauth2` stays next to the indented block it introduces. M130b2 shipped that diagnostic and this is its first consumer.)

## `M130-08` — found by breaking it

Adding `authorized target` to the root config turned TF060's fixture red:

```
✗ TF060: tests/.checkonly/security-without-authorized-target.tflw reports TF060
  — 1 file checked, no problems found.
```

A `.checkonly` fixture is checked from the repo root, so it reads the **root** config, and TF060 fires on the **absence** of a declaration. That proof silently depended on the shared config never having one. Nothing in the fixture recorded the dependency and nothing in `tflw.config` warned that adding a line would break a proof in another file — **a dependency on an absence has no natural place to be declared, so it wasn't.**

`TF051` and `TF057`/`TF058` already argue this exact case in the same script, in their own headers. TF060 was the instance nobody had converted. It now has its own scratch-config pair, which also buys a case the old form could not express at all: the **positive** direction, where a declared target silences the diagnostic. An absence-based proof can only ever assert the absence.

It went red rather than quiet, which is the only reason this is a closed row and not a silent hole.

## Verified on fedora-box, fresh stack

- full suite **322/322**, `ok: true`
- all **55** TF0xx codes the installed tflw assigns are still dogfooded; both TF060 directions green
- `verify:ledger` — 286 rows / 57 open / 221 closed, re-derived
- suite-wide authz blind spot: **29 of 1019 api steps** declare an owner

That last number is the one worth carrying into the guide: §0(b)'s bound is not a caveat, it is the dominant fact about this tier's reach on a real suite.

body:
Two bits of CI hygiene, both pre-existing on `main`, independent of #286.

## 1. The stale assertion — why `e2e` has been red

`e2e/deck.spec.mjs` asserted the breathing pill as a **headcount**:

```js
return breathing.length === 1 && breathing[0].dataset.status === "waiting";
//     "the waiting lock breathes; no other mark animates"
```

#283 then gave the **locked** pill the same pulse when a style proposal sits behind the lock — the door-with-no-handle fix, because a locked chunk had no way to say something was waiting inside:

```js
waiting: "… motion-safe:animate-lock-breathe",                              // PILL.waiting
const STYLE_PILL = "ring-2 ring-pending motion-safe:animate-lock-breathe";  // the LOCKED pill
```

Two marks breathe by design now, so `length === 1` has been false on **every run since that merge**. The deck fixture contains exactly such a chunk — the spec asserts as much two checks later — which is why this is deterministic, not flaky. Confirmed identical on `main`'s own run [`31639882505`](https://github.com/wilplus/frontend-cursor/actions/runs/31639882505) at `67f2930a` and on a re-run of #286's head SHA.

**The feature was right; the test was stale.** Rewritten as the rule the pulse actually encodes — *something here wants you* — instead of a headcount:

- every breathing mark is either the waiting chunk **or** a locked one wearing the style ring;
- at least one waiting chunk breathes;
- a settled `clean` mark never does — the half the original was really protecting, kept exactly.

Stated as an invariant, a third legitimate breather won't break it again.

## 2. The stray gitlink

`.claude/worktrees/naughty-leakey-4b222c` is a mode `160000` entry with no `.gitmodules` record, committed in #194 on 2026-07-30. `actions/checkout`'s cleanup has printed `fatal: No url found for submodule path …` and exited 128 on every run of every branch since.

`.gitignore` already lists `.claude/worktrees/` — that rule landed *after* the commit, and `.gitignore` never untracks what is already tracked. `git rm --cached` is the missing half.

## 3. `continue-on-error` — deliberately NOT changed, and I'd like a decision

You asked why a failing `e2e` job doesn't fail the run. It does not, **on purpose**, and the workflow header says so:

> `e2e` — … **NON-BLOCKING (continue-on-error) for an observation period** — real-browser timing can flake in CI, and a gate that cries wolf gets ignored. **Flip it blocking once it has a quiet track record.**

So this is a policy with a stated exit condition, not a misconfiguration. I have left `continue-on-error: true` in place, because flipping it **today** — the day we discovered the tier has been silently red on a stale assertion — would be against that condition rather than in service of it. There is no quiet track record yet; this PR is what makes one possible.

**Recommendation:** merge this, watch `e2e` go green and stay green for a handful of runs on `main`, then flip `continue-on-error` off in a one-line follow-up. That is the documented plan, arrived at on schedule.

Worth noting either way: the failure was invisible because the *run* reported **success** while the *job* reported **failure**. That is the same shape as the silent-zero lanes cleaned up in the backend today — a real red hiding under a green tick — and it is the argument for eventually flipping the flag.

## Verification

`node --check` on the spec · `tsc --noEmit` clean · vitest **1231 passed** (98 files).

**The deck spec itself could not be run locally** — it times out waiting on the `/dev/deck` harness in this sandbox, on `main` as well as on this branch, so the environment rather than the change. The rewritten assertion is therefore verified **by CI on this PR**, not locally. If `e2e` is still red here, the rewrite is wrong and I will say so.

`FILTER: JUSTIFIED-SCAFFOLDING — cat {SCAFFOLDING} — fences {clear} — locks {clear} — redirect: restores e2e as a trustworthy gate, which is what the swap-lane FE work lands against`

author: sergiussidorov
body:
ST-3 of the two-ADR feature: the sender stops retrying and starts reporting. Scope is `push2u-core` and `push2u-spring-boot-starter`; the Vault module was ST-2's and is untouched here.

Refs #86
Refs #87

## What changed

**`PushOutcome` replaces `PushResult`** as a sealed hierarchy: `Accepted` (RFC 8030 §5 — accepted for delivery, not received), `SubscriptionExpired`, `RetryableFailure(statusCode, retryAfter)`, `NonRetryableFailure`, the `NotAttempted` marker with `SignerUnavailable`, `PayloadRejected` and `EndpointRejected` implementing it directly, and `Indeterminate` for the unanswered POST. `SignerUnavailable` and `Indeterminate` are classes with written `toString()` and identity equality (written down on the type); nothing prints a capability URL by default, and each `cause()` documents what its chain may contain.

**The status matrix is per status**: `2xx` accepted; `404`/`410` expired; `408`, `421`, `429` and the 5xx class except `501`, `505`, `506`, `508`, `511` retryable; `413` retryable exactly when it carries a parseable `Retry-After`; everything else not. `507` is named retryable against the pull of its class; `510` is deliberately unnamed and falls to the unnamed-5xx rule. Every carve-out carries its defining specification's own words in the variants' Javadoc, since a `sources.jar` reader has no repository.

**The retry machinery is gone**: the loop, `RetryPolicy`, `Sleeper`, `Builder.retryPolicy`, the package-private `Builder.sleeper` seam, the trailing `AssertionError`, `push2u.retry.*` with `Push2uProperties.Retry` and the `requireValid` probes. `Ticker` stays (token cache). `RetryAfter` stays package-private and unchanged; its parsed output is now published on the retryable variant, with no ceiling applied.

**The facade converts three seam types and no others** — `PushDeliveryException` → `Indeterminate`, `EndpointRejectedException` → `EndpointRejected`, `VapidSignerUnavailableException` → `SignerUnavailable`; any other `RuntimeException` propagates as a defect. The conversion is refused on both paths when the cause chain carries an `InterruptedException` or the thread's interrupt status is set; what leaves is `PushInterruptedException` with the flag re-set before the throw, and on `sendAsync` a future that completes exceptionally and is not cancelled.

**`PayloadRejected` reports plaintext octets**: the payload handed over against the smaller of (body ceiling − 103) and (rs − 18), computed in `WebPushEncryptor.maxPlaintextBytes` — the same subtraction `checkRecordSize` now inverts, so the RFC 8291 §4 rule keeps one implementation.

**Three facts are stated where a caller meets them**: the unclamped `Retry-After` on `RetryableFailure` (and on `SignerUnavailable.retryAfter()`); RFC 8030 §5.2's TTL re-basing on `send` and on `RetryableFailure`; the stop-the-fan-out advice on `SignerUnavailable`, in both the sequential (`break`) and the asynchronous form (bound the concurrency, feed rows in as outcomes come back, stop submitting once one arrived), with `sendAsync` pointing at it.

## Prose rewritten under the three-shape rule

Named-what-a-send-throws / reasoned-from-the-retry-window / used-the-status-versus-exception oracle:

- `PushSender` class Javadoc, `send` and `sendAsync` `@throws` and bodies (all three shapes)
- `EndpointRejectedException` — "worth retrying" / "IAE means an oversized payload" contrast
- `PushDeliveryException` — the `PushResult` reference and what a caller of `send` sees
- `EndpointPolicy` (twice) and `EndpointPolicies.unrestricted()` — the SSRF oracle restated as outcome-status versus `Indeterminate`; plus the "3xx surfaces as a failed PushResult" sentence
- `PushHttpClient` — "the PushSender owns retry and status interpretation", and the 3xx classification sentence
- `JdkPushHttpClient` — "classifies as a failed PushResult"
- `PushResponse` — the negative-sentinel rationale that pointed at `PushResult`
- `Builder.executor(...)` — the backoff-sleeps reasoning
- `Builder.jwtRenewBefore(...)` — the margin's derivation from `RetryPolicy#maxBackoff()` (retained value, restated ground: clock skew plus transport timeouts the library does not own)
- `Builder.recordSize` / `maxEncryptedBodyBytes` — refusals now described as the outcome, not an IAE
- `Ticker` — "for the same reason `Sleeper` is"
- `RetryAfter` — three sentences reasoning from the deleted computed backoff and the retry count
- `Push2uHealthAutoConfiguration` — `RetryPolicy` in the list of immutable sender configuration
- `checkstyleReferences`-visible test prose updated where it described the removed behaviour (`JdkPushHttpClientFailureTest`, JWT suites)

## Suites rewritten rather than adjusted

`PushSenderStatusClassificationTest` (now the per-status matrix, one POST asserted per case), `PushSenderTest` (Retry-After honouring became Retry-After reporting), `PushSenderPayloadSizeTest`, `PushSenderEndpointPolicyTest` (rejection is a value; async completes normally with it), `BcFipsPushSenderTest`, and the fixtures that fed the loop several answers — `MockPushReceiver` now serves one configured response, `PushTestSupport` lost `RecordingSleeper`. New: `PushOutcomeTest`, `PushSenderSeamConversionTest` (conversions, propagation, interruption on both paths, sync and async). Deleted: `RetryPolicyTest`, `SleeperTest`. `RetryAfterTest` stays untouched — it calls the unchanged parser directly.

## Judgement calls left open by the ADR

- `EndpointRejected` carries two components: a library-computed `redactedEndpoint` (safe by construction) beside the policy's `reason` (whose seam contract already forbids the raw endpoint) — "a redacted endpoint or a structured reason" read as both, so the caller keeps the which-rule-refused diagnostic without the library vouching for consumer prose.
- `SignerUnavailable` is constructed from the `VapidSignerUnavailableException` itself and delegates `status()`/`retryAfter()` to it — the outcome cannot disagree with the seam signal, and no Optional-typed constructor parameters exist.
- Variant validation kept at what `PushResult`'s compact constructor applied (non-negative status; plus non-null/non-negative hint and non-negative sizes) rather than range-pinning each variant — the ADR's `RetryableFailure(413, empty)` precedent.
- The interruption walk guards against a cyclic cause chain (identity set), so a defective seam cannot hang a send.
- `PMD.GodClass` joined the facade's existing `CouplingBetweenObjects` suppression with the reason extended: the classification and the conversion enumeration are the facade's own, and scattering them would split the one list the interrupt discipline depends on.
- SpotBugs `EI_EXPOSE_REP` on the two `cause()` accessors is excluded in `config/quality/spotbugs/exclusions.xml` with the reason: handing back the seam's own `Throwable` is the accessor's documented contract.

## Gates

`./gradlew qualityCheck` and `./gradlew javadoc` both green with zero warnings, on this branch's state and again after rebasing onto the feature branch with ST-2 merged — the Vault Testcontainers test ran against a live Docker daemon. With ST-2 in the base, `SignerUnavailable` has its first shipped producer; the conversion tests here still use a test double on purpose, and the end-to-end pairing is the feature-level review's to exercise.

## Summary
- route staged verified GGUF downloads through the embedded runtime even while their resumable filename ends in `.gguf.partial`

- staged/final GGUF and legacy GGML runtime routing
- current-vs-legacy model inventory projection

- automatic deletion of legacy GGML files

`ArtifactFormat` is now explicit trusted metadata carried by runtime manifests, installation candidates, the isolated verifier process, and runtime models. The router no longer infers the runtime from the final path extension, so a pinned `*.gguf.partial` candidate remains an embedded GGUF.

body:
## Summary

N3.5 — fixes the three forward hazards carried from #93 so **N4's `nightly.yaml` does not fail its first base crawl**. Ships alone, no workflow yet.

```
N1 578042d  #91 — deep-inspect schema _ab          DONE
N2 80fa3be  #92 — VERSION_RE / SYNTHETIC_VERSIONS  DONE
N3 626d3bd  #93 — nightly-build.ts                  DONE
N3.5 this  — per-phase gates + outs.find fix       ← NEW (unblocks N4)
N4 — nightly.yaml (discover gate → x86+arm64, 1 boot / 2 crawls each) — next
```

### Forward hazards fixed (from #93 re-review)

**1. `argsTotal` floor was phase-blind — would fail base crawl**
`floor = arch==arm64?34000:33000` is calibrated for the full-package set, but stable `7.24rc4` is `base 28,079` vs `extra 35,656`. Nightly `ab431` full extra is `x86 33,685 / arm64 34,735` — base would be ~28k and `28k < 33k` → fail.

Fix: `getArgsTotalFloor(arch, phase)` → `base 25k/26k`, `extra/all 33k/34k`. Floors are deliberately conservative (not near median) — calibrated from the numbers above. The old floor failing `28,079` is now covered by a test.

**2. `outs.find(f => f.startsWith("deep-inspect."))` was ambiguous**
With N4's `one boot / two crawls` the tmpDir will hold both `deep-inspect.nightly-quickchr-x86-base.json` and `deep-inspect.nightly-quickchr-x86.json`; first readdir match would silently gate the wrong file.

Fix: `buildOutputSuffix(arch, phase, custom?)` → `nightly-quickchr-x86` for `all/extra`, `nightly-quickchr-x86-base` for `base` (custom suffix overrides). Gate now selects `expectedFile = deep-inspect.<outputSuffix>.json` first, with fallback to prefix → generic. Adds a collision test showing old code always picking base.

**3. No `--phase` — script always uploaded full NPK set + single crawl**
N4 needs `routeros-* → base` then `remaining → extra/` (1 boot / 2 crawls, #90 §6). Extra phase without `routeros-*` alone would leave mixed versions, so `extra` / `all` both mean full set (5 x86 / 9 arm64) while `base` means `routeros-*` only (1 NPK).

Fix: `--phase base|extra|all` (default `all`) + `--output-suffix <str>` override. `getNpksForPhase()` handles the split, `getExpectedMinPackageCount()` makes the package-count gate phase-aware (`1` vs `5/9`), download/upload/logs/provenance all respect `PHASE`.

### Other wiring

* `nightly.json` provenance records `phase`, `phaseFiles`, `outputSuffix`; `packages` now has `phase`, `count` (phase count), `allArchCount`, `rejected` narrow (still 1 plausible generic duplicate).
* `--dry-run` now shows `[phase=..., suffix=...]` and lists `all for arch:` when filtered.
* `tmpDir` still per-run; distinct suffixes let base+extra coexist in one dir when N4 does sequential crawls (or N4 can pass explicit `--output-suffix x86-base` / `x86`).

### Tests & gates

* 11 nightly tests (was 6) — new `phase-aware helpers` describe block covers `getNpksForPhase`, `getExpectedMinPackageCount`, `getArgsTotalFloor` (including the `28,079 < 33,000` base-fail case), `buildOutputSuffix`, and the `outs.find` collision.
* `bun test` 226 pass (was 221), `tsc --noEmit` 0, `biome check` 0. No `inspect.json` shape change.

### Provenance shape delta for N4

N4 will aggregate `x86 base`, `x86 extra`, `arm64 base`, `arm64 extra` into the single `docs/nightly/` slot per #90 §6 (base `inspect.json` is x86 routeros-only, `extra/` is full). This PR gives it the primitives (`--phase`, per-phase floors, suffix) to do so without a second CHR boot per arch if desired; a two-boot first version (base job + extra job) also works since floors are now correct.

Closes the N3→N4 gap noted in #90#5284814141.

author: wshlavacek
body:
Fixes #569.

`job_type = check` has not started since #565 landed. Every run dies in setup:

```
Sorry, an unknown error occurred: AttributeError: 'ModelCheck' object has no attribute 'res_dir'
```

#564's method-chain record is built at `pybnf.py:667` from `alg.res_dir`, on a line that runs unconditionally — nine lines *above* the `fit_type != 'check'` branch that exists precisely because the check path is not an algorithm run. The check path reaches the record first and dies there, so the job produces no objective value at all. It is not a noisy tail; the fit type does not start.

## Two crash sites, not one

Guarding line 667 alone only moves the failure nine lines down. The fit-phase recording added by the same commit reads three more `Algorithm` attributes:

```python
        fit_status, fit_reason = _phase_status(alg)          # alg.stop_reason
        _record_phase(alg, 'fit', config.config['fit_type'], fit_status, reason=fit_reason,
                      simulations=alg.completed_simulations,
                      best_objective=alg.trajectory.best_score() if len(alg.trajectory) else None)
```

`ModelCheck` deliberately does not subclass `Algorithm` — its docstring says so, and the branch in `main()` is the consequence — so it has none of the four:

```
>>> [hasattr(alg, a) for a in ('res_dir', 'stop_reason', 'completed_simulations', 'trajectory')]
[False, False, False, False]
```

Both sites now sit inside the branch, with the boundary stated in a comment so the next addition to `main()` lands on the correct side of it.

## What is deliberately unchanged

**A check run still writes no `method_chain.json`.** It is one evaluation of the parameters as given, not a chain of search phases; its `phases` / `simulations` / `best_objective` / `stop_reason` would all be empty or invented. #564 exists to make provenance assertable, not to pad it.

**`alg.budget` stays where it is.** It is not a latent copy of the same bug: assigning an attribute to a `ModelCheck` is legal, and `Configuration._strip_uncheckable_keys` pops `wall_time_fit` before the defaults are applied, so `from_config` returns `None` and the budget block below it is skipped — no misleading "Wall-time budget for this fit" line on a job with no run to budget. That same strip is what keeps `_refine_best_fit` and `_run_bootstrapping` no-ops on the check path, which is why neither of them broke.

## Why nothing caught it

`job_type = check` has tests, and every one of them calls `run_check()` directly — which was never the part that broke. `tests/full_tests/T6-check/` is referenced by no test module and no workflow. So two commits (35a2dc04, b8c05769) landed on top of a fit type that could not start.

The regression test added here drives a `job_type = check` job end to end through `main()` and asserts it exits 0 and reports its objective value. It needs no simulator: the model is a zero-dimensional analytical menu target scored through `objective = score`, which makes the reported objective an exact `0.0` the test can assert on. Verified to fail on b8c05769 with the reported `AttributeError` and to pass here.

## Verification

* `tests/test_model_check.py::test_a_check_job_run_through_main_reports_an_objective_value` — fails on the parent commit, passes with the fix.
* Full default-tier suite: **3776 passed, 20 skipped, 186 deselected** (13:57), with `BNGPATH` set.
* `ruff check` clean.

author: satriadhm
body:
**Stacked on #11.** Base is `feat/oauth-resource-metadata`, so this diff is two commits. Merge #11 first.

**Needs the Studio's authorization server deployed FIRST** (dreambooth#577). The metadata here points at a discovery document that has to already exist; a discovery chain that dead-ends is worse than no discovery.

## Why

The submission portal said *"We couldn't detect OAuth metadata from this MCP URL"*, and it was right. Three separate causes, each sufficient on its own.

**The protected-resource document is published where nothing looks for it.** RFC 9728 §3.1 inserts the resource's path into the well-known URL, so a resource at `/mcp` publishes at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp`. Clients construct that URL themselves. Only the bare path existed.

**It was never live either.** `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` returns 404 on the production host today, because #11 is unmerged. The rejected submission was reviewed against a build with no discovery document at all. Curled, not assumed.

**And nothing ever returned 401.** A client does not go looking for an authorization server on a hunch. It discovers one because a request came back 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming where the resource metadata lives. Without that, this connector is indistinguishable from one that needs no authentication, which is exactly what was concluded.

## What changed

- Both spellings of the protected-resource path, plus a **307** from `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` on this host to the Studio. A redirect rather than a copy: serving the Studio's document from here would publish metadata whose `issuer` does not match the URL it came from, and RFC 8414 §3 requires a client to reject exactly that.
- **A per-tool 401**, not a per-request one, and that distinction is the whole design. `initialize`, `tools/list` and `search_docs` still answer anonymously, so the listing's promise that hardware and pricing questions need no account stays true and positive test case 5 still passes with nothing connected. Only the seven tools that talk to the Studio challenge.
- `toolAuth.ts` **fails open** on anything ambiguous (a batch, a malformed body, an unknown tool name). 401ing a request that was never a tool call takes the connector down entirely; missing one merely restores today's behaviour.
- **An `Authorization` header now wins over any session, and is never merged into one.** A credential that arrived on this request belongs to this request; writing it into a session store would leave it readable by every later request quoting the same session id. Sessions that completed the device flow are unaffected because they already hold a token, which is what lets the Electron booth's flow and OAuth coexist rather than one replacing the other.
- `connect_account` no longer tells stateless clients that signing in cannot work here. It can now; it just happens in the client's own connector settings.

## Verification

Against a running server:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| 4 discovery paths | 200 / 200 / 307 / 307 |
| `get_credits`, no token | **401** + `WWW-Authenticate` naming the path-suffixed metadata URL |
| `initialize`, no token | 200 |
| `search_docs`, no token | 200 |

Plus 7 new tests over the gate that decides which of those a request gets, and `tsc` clean across src and scripts.

**Not verified:** a real client completing the flow end to end. That needs both this and dreambooth#577 deployed.

author: coopersully
body:
## Overview

Separates connected-agent authority from workspace setup so Settings identifies the one action a person must take without repeating completed steps, operational queues, or agent-owned work. Readiness evidence now puts unresolved checks first and keeps completed history quiet, while MCP application links fail closed onto the canonical production Ilo origin instead of silently pointing agents at localhost.

### Work map

- **Issue:** Closes #130 — completes the workspace settings, actionable review, and production MCP link acceptance criteria.
- **Reference:** [Workspace settings separation and MCP link integrity design](https://github.com/coopersully/personal-os/blob/cooper/debug-production-ilo-finance-mcp/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-13-workspace-settings-and-mcp-links-design.md) — approved information architecture, ownership, compatibility, and rollout contract.

## Why this change

- **Problem:** Workspace Access mixed credential scope, readiness, setup, and review state. Workspace Settings then repeated the same setup action as a summary, readiness next step, alert, checklist step, and operational-review count. Completed checks visually competed with work that remained, and readiness copy repeated workspace names and implementation detail. Finance could also report a guidance draft needing review without exposing the approval there, and production MCP metadata could emit localhost application links.
- **Safety rules:** Workspace configuration approvals remain signed-in Ilo actions; operational email and finance cases remain in their owning workspaces; agent scopes and financial mutation authority are unchanged.
- **Approach:** Keep Workspace Access access-only, derive one person-owned action from the server setup plan, mirror it in navigation with Shadcn sidebar badges, keep readiness diagnostic, route review actions to their domain Settings sections, and centralize validated MCP application links with deployment-time configuration enforcement.

## What changed

- Added accessible **Action required** badges to Mail, Finances, Calendar, and Tasks Settings navigation on desktop and mobile when the current setup step belongs to the signed-in person.
- Reduced each workspace Settings page to one current person-owned action with one direct control. Removed completed and waiting setup steps, duplicate setup wrappers, completed-state reassurance banners, and operational review counts from Settings.
- Refined the shared readiness panel to show **N to finish**, **N of N complete**, and **Review checks**. Its dialog now lists unresolved checks first with full evidence and actions, while completed checks are collapsed by default into compact muted history.
- Shortened workspace readiness titles and evidence copy to local, direct labels such as **Accounts**, **Rules**, **Workflow**, and **Agent access**.
- Removed operational attention queues from readiness calculations. Open review items remain work in their owning workspace and no longer inflate or contradict setup status.
- Suppressed readiness focus when the page action already owns the same next step, preventing a second copy of the task.
- Removed the duplicate Finance guidance link to agent connections; the shared page action is now the one authoritative connection control.
- Reduced Workspace Access to observed connected-host authority and human-readable capability boundaries. Moved Calendar source controls under Calendar Settings.
- Added neutral per-item capability markers in Workspace Access: check circle for Allowed, hand for Needs your approval, and x circle for Not allowed. Labels and descriptions remain unchanged.
- Preserved unsaved Finance profile edits across background refreshes and show agent-owned setup steps as **Setup in progress** without creating person-action badges.
- Moved Finance guidance approval and the financial profile into Finance Settings; the legacy profile route redirects to the exact guidance surface. Operational Finance review remains under Finance.
- Routed Mail rule review links from Reviews to the Mail Settings dialog.
- Centralized MCP application link construction, rejected missing or unsafe production origins, and removed implicit localhost fallbacks from HTTP and stdio metadata.
- Injected and exactly validated `APP_BASE_URL` in every rendered MCP task definition during deployment.
- Strengthened post-render deployment validation to require exactly one `APP_BASE_URL` entry whose value matches the canonical application origin.

## Documentation

- Updated: [design system](https://github.com/coopersully/personal-os/blob/cooper/debug-production-ilo-finance-mcp/docs/design/system.md) — records the person-owned navigation badge, single-action composition, readiness hierarchy, and completed-check disclosure rules.
- Updated: [workspace settings and MCP design](https://github.com/coopersully/personal-os/blob/cooper/debug-production-ilo-finance-mcp/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-13-workspace-settings-and-mcp-links-design.md) — records page ownership, review boundaries, action deduplication, checklist hierarchy, legacy redirects, accessibility, and production link integrity.
- Updated the agent-access action-queue design to match the shared **Review checks** disclosure.

## Verification

| Check | What it proves |
| --- | --- |
| `pnpm verify` | Environment contracts, lint, types, 683 tests across 81 files, 96.67% statement/line coverage, 95.72% function coverage, 94.05% branch coverage, production builds, and all 6 desktop/mobile Playwright acceptance tests pass |
| `pnpm exec vitest run apps/web/src/components/readiness-panel.test.tsx apps/web/src/features/agent-access/readiness.test.ts apps/web/src/features/settings/agent-access.test.tsx` | The unresolved-first dialog, collapsed completed checks, concise workspace evidence, operational-queue removal, and action deduplication regressions pass |

### Manual checks

- Exercised Mail and Finance Settings against the running full-data demo fixture at `localhost:8101`.
- Confirmed all four current person-owned setup actions have accessible sidebar badges.
- Confirmed the Mail readiness overview uses direct counts and opens with only outstanding checks visible.
- Confirmed expanding completed checks reveals compact muted history, and closing the dialog resets that disclosure.
- Confirmed operational review counts no longer appear as setup evidence and Workspace Access remains access-only.

## Boundary analysis

- **Durable commit point:** No asynchronous provider work is added. Deployment registers an MCP task definition only after its rendered environment contains exactly one canonical `APP_BASE_URL`; MCP validates that origin before serving.
- **Production disconfirming case:** Correct task configuration can still coexist with a bad DNS, TLS, load-balancer, or cached remote-host path after deployment.
- **Evidence:** Unit tests prove URL parsing and allowlisted paths; static deployment contracts prove injection and exact-value validation; builds and local MCP tests prove both entry points use the shared resolver.
- **Remaining proof:** After merge and deployment, the release owner must make a non-mutating production MCP call and confirm every `_ilo.links` value uses `https://app.ilo.coopersully.me`, then observe normal service health.

## Scope and limitations

- Navigation badges currently reflect the server setup plan's current person-owned step; operational review queues do not create Settings badges.
- This PR does not create a recurring Finance automation; monthly-review guidance is explicitly labelled as guidance only.
- It does not grant agents transaction-edit or money-movement authority.
- Production behavior changes only after merge and deployment; the post-deploy MCP smoke remains required.
